subs.title: Resource-owning type from a blank file

c.v: Take 60 minutes, closed book, from a blank file. Build a class
that creates a uniquely named file inside a directory you are given, and removes that file from disk when the object is destroyed, unless the caller has said to keep it.
creates a new, empty file in
, opens it for writing, and throws if the file cannot be created.
marks the file to survive the object, and

returns where it lives, so a test can check it. The type owns a real resource, so it follows the rule of five rather than the rule of zero: work out for yourself which of the five special members you need and what each must do, rather than starting from a member that already has them.
Write your own tests for these, and run them under
; nothing here needs a second thread.

items.v: The file exists while the object is alive and is gone once its scope ends.
, writes a line and then throws still has the file removed by the time the exception is caught, wherever it is caught.
before the object is destroyed leaves the file on disk, and your test removes it afterwards so the run leaves nothing behind.
transfers ownership: destroying the moved-from source first does not touch the file, and only the destination's eventual destruction removes it.

onto another removes the file the target held, as well as taking on the source's file, and assigning an object to itself through a function that takes two references to it leaves the file exactly as it was.

c.v: A strong answer at 60 minutes has all five special members, each doing one job: the constructor never leaves a caller holding a failed file, the destructor releases exactly once, copying is refused rather than silently allowed, and both moves leave a moved-from object safe to destroy without touching anything. All five tests above pass, and the run is clean under AddressSanitizer. A partial answer gets the single-object behaviour right, tests 1 to 4, but move assignment onto an already-open target either leaks the old file or forgets the self-assignment guard, which test 5 is built to catch. A fail is a class that can still be copied, so two objects fight over deleting the same path, or a destructor that never removes the file at all, which passes every test that only checks existence while the object is alive and none of them notice.

subs.title: Bounded queue with shutdown from a blank file

c.v: Take 60 minutes, closed book, from a blank file. Build
, a bounded blocking queue whose shutdown is per caller rather than queue-wide: every call to
flag the way the plain bounded queue does.
waits while the queue is full, hands the item over and returns true, or returns false without adding it if
waits while the queue is empty, takes the oldest item and returns it, or returns no value if

fires while it is still empty. An item already in the queue is always handed over, even to a call whose token has already fired: the wait drains before it gives up, the same rule the plain bounded queue's
, the one with the overload that takes a token, on both waits. Write your own tests for these:

items.v: Push twice into a queue of capacity two with a token that is never stopped, then push a third time with an already-stopped
's token: the third call returns false at once rather than waiting, because the queue is full and the stop has already fired.
Pop the queue down by one, then push again with the same never-stopped token: it succeeds, because there is room again.
Push one item, then request a stop on a fresh
with its token: the call still returns that item. Pop again with the same stopped token on the now-empty queue: it returns no value.
Several producer threads pushing with tokens that are never stopped, and several consumer threads popping with one

shared between them, requested only once every producer thread has been joined. Check that every item sent is received exactly once, sorted ids match a plain count from zero, and the queue is left empty. Add a watcher thread that samples
in a tight loop through the run and keeps the largest value it saw, and check it never passed the capacity.
Build the stress test from point 4 a second time with
, in a job of its own, and run it more than once.

c.v: A strong answer at 60 minutes has both waits carrying the token into
rather than a hand-rolled loop that polls

on its own, gets the five tests above to pass, and comes back clean under both sanitizers. A partial answer gets the single-threaded behaviour right but polls the token in a loop with a timed wait instead of using the predicate-and-token overload, which works but wastes CPU and is harder to reason about under contention. A fail is a queue that still carries a

flag set by some member function, which answers a different question than the one this task asks, or one where a stopped consumer's wait can also cancel a producer's, because the two waits share one condition variable instead of one each.
The single-threaded behaviour first, which is where the token-and-predicate contract is easiest to see:

c.v: Every run prints the same three lines and exits 0: nothing here depends on which thread the scheduler favours, only on totals and an invariant, so ThreadSanitizer has nothing to report and the output has nothing to disagree with either.

Take 15 minutes. For each of the two builds, write down your time against the 60 minutes, whether AddressSanitizer, and for the queue ThreadSanitizer too, came back clean, and which of the tests listed above passed on the first run. Add one line naming the single weakest part of what you wrote: the special member you got wrong first, or the test you had to add after a run failed rather than before it. You pass this assessment when both builds are clean under their sanitizers and every listed test passes, from a blank file, without notes. A build that only compiles after checking a page is not ready to be marked passed; note which page it was and revisit that topic's exercises before the next attempt.
